scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that favours the public's right to know while granting rare security exceptions; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Governments constantly decide how much of the truth to share with the people they serve.
Some believe leaders may rightly withhold information from the public, while others insist the public has a right to be fully informed.
I lean strongly toward the public's right to know, though I accept that a few rare cases may justify secrecy.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why the public has a right to know

sentences.text: First, in a free society, people generally have a right to know what their leaders are doing.
Citizens cannot make wise choices at elections if important facts are hidden from them.
For example, a government that hides a public health danger leaves people unable to protect themselves.
This shows that secrecy can rob citizens of the knowledge they need to act and to vote.
Open information also keeps leaders honest, since they know their actions can be examined.
When the public is kept in the dark, the abuse of power becomes far easier to hide.
For these reasons, the right to be informed is a vital part of a healthy society.

sections.role: Body 2 — When secrecy may be justified

sentences.text: Second, however, the opposing view is right that a few situations may justify withholding information.
Some military or security secrets, if revealed, could put many innocent lives in danger.
Consider plans for defending a country, which would be useless if every detail were made public.
Such cases show that total openness is not always safe or wise.
Releasing certain information too early could also cause needless panic before the facts are clear.
These exceptions, however, must be rare and clearly justified, not a habit of hiding the truth.
Secrecy, then, should be the rare exception rather than the normal rule.
In conclusion, I firmly support the public's right to be fully informed.
But the opposing view rightly notes that genuine matters of safety may sometimes require secrecy.
The best balance keeps government open by default while allowing narrow, well-justified exceptions.
